1071.quote_or_event: “They belong to the human species, but they act like animals.”
1071.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan describes people who are human by birth but whose conduct is that of beasts.
1071.tie_back: The Kural ironically says the base look exactly like human beings; Guru Arjan makes the same point, that a human form can hide conduct that is not human at all.
1071.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 267, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1071._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: both say the base share the human form but not human character; only the Kural's ironic tone is missing.

1072.quote_or_event: “The world is asleep in Maya, the house of Shakti; it dances, jumps and sings in duality. The self-willed manmukh has no devotion.”
1072.explanation: Guru Amar Das pictures the world as carefree and dancing while it is really asleep in Maya (worldly illusion), and says the self-willed person (manmukh) has no devotion.
1072.tie_back: The Kural sarcastically calls the base luckier than the wise because nothing troubles them; Guru Amar Das shows that this carefree dancing is really the sleep of people lost in illusion.
1072.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 506, Raag Gujri, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1072._accuracy_note: Partial fit: it explains why the careless seem untroubled, but it speaks of the whole worldly-minded world, not of base people in particular, and lacks the Kural's sarcasm.

1073.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, it is written that you shall obey the Hukam of His Command, and walk in the Way of His Will.”
1073.explanation: The first pauri of Japji Sahib teaches that the true person lives within hukam, the divine order, rather than by his own will.
1073.tie_back: The Kural mocks the base as godlike because they too do whatever they please; Guru Nanak sets the opposite ideal, a life that walks in God's will instead of one's own wishes.
1073.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib (pauri 1), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1073._accuracy_note: Next-best match given as a contrast: Sikh teaching condemns acting by self-will (manmukh) but has no parallel to the Kural's ironic comparison with the gods.

1074.quote_or_event: “One who calls himself good - goodness shall not draw near him.”
1074.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan warns that self-praise is a sign of haumai (ego), and that goodness keeps away from the person who declares himself good.
1074.tie_back: The Kural shows the base swelling with pride when they meet people worse than themselves; Guru Arjan says that whoever rates himself as good is thereby cut off from goodness.
1074.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1074._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the self-flattering pride of the base; Guru Arjan states it as a general rule about ego rather than as a comparison with worse people.

1075.quote_or_event: “One who does not frighten anyone, and who is not afraid of anyone else”
1075.explanation: In his saloks, Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the truly wise person as one who neither frightens others nor is ruled by fear of them.
1075.tie_back: The Kural says the base behave well mainly out of fear of punishment; Guru Tegh Bahadur's ideal person acts rightly without being driven by fear at all.
1075.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1427, Saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1075._accuracy_note: Next-best match given as a contrast: it sets fearless goodness against fear-driven conduct but does not address greed, the Kural's second motive.

1076.quote_or_event: “The impurity of the ears is to listen to the slander of others.”
1076.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak lists the real impurities of each sense, and says that of the ears is listening to tale-bearing and slander about others.
1076.tie_back: The Kural compares the base to a town crier's drum that spreads every secret it hears; Guru Nanak names the eager ear for gossip and tale-bearing as a real impurity.
1076.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 472, Raag Asa, Asa di Vaar (salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1076._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: Guru Nanak condemns listening to tale-bearing, while the Kural condemns repeating secrets.

1077.quote_or_event: The Sikh langar, the free communal kitchen attached to every gurdwara, serves food to all who come. Britannica notes that everyone sits in a line with no place of higher or lower rank, and that Guru Amar Das required visitors to eat in this casteless langar.
1077.explanation: The langar puts vand chhakna (sharing what one has) into practice: food is given freely and equally, without asking who the guest is.
1077.tie_back: The Kural says the base will not even shake crumbs from their wet hand except for those who would break their jaw; the langar stands for the opposite, food shared freely with everyone without any pressure.
1077._accuracy_note: Next-best match given as a contrast to the miser's grudging hand; it is an institution, not a teaching about base people, and Britannica notes that its early origins are not fully documented.

1078.quote_or_event: “One who performs selfless service, without thought of reward, shall attain his Lord and Master.”
1078.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan praises seva done freely, without any wish for return.
1078.tie_back: The Kural says the noble help as soon as they are told of a need, while the base give only when crushed like sugarcane; Guru Arjan praises service given freely, with no need to be forced or rewarded.
1078.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286, Raag Gauri, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1078._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit for the noble half of the couplet; it does not mention the base, and seva in Sikhism is first of all service of the Guru and the sangat.

1079.quote_or_event: “Fareed, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
1079.explanation: In a salok included in the Guru Granth Sahib, Sheikh Farid tells the clever person to stop listing other people's faults and to examine his own.
1079.tie_back: The Kural says the base become experts at finding fault when they see others well clothed and fed; Farid's salok tells the fault-finder to look at himself instead.
1079.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Saloks of Sheikh Farid (salok 6) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1079._accuracy_note: Strong fit on fault-finding; Farid does not mention the envy of others' comfort that sets it off in the Kural.

1080.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand.”
1080.explanation: In a salok, Guru Nanak says the path of love for God is open only to someone ready to give his life. Sikhs read this as the root of the Gurus' readiness for martyrdom.
1080.tie_back: The Kural says the base are good only for selling themselves the moment trouble comes; Guru Nanak's ideal is the opposite, a person who comes with head in hand and will not sell out at any price.
1080.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaran te Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1080._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit given as a contrast: it sets total commitment against the base person's readiness to sell himself, but it speaks of devotion rather than of baseness.
